spoken_segments.text: All right. Hi everyone. I'm excited to be here and today I'm going to chat about the evolution of software factoring. Software engineering and how it's becoming factory engineering, so excited to do this.

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker introduces himself and the central topic of the presentation on the main stage.

scenes.visual_summary: Introductory slide introducing Zach Lloyd with bullet points detailing his experience at Google Docs, 20 years in engineering, and founding Warp.
ocr_details: Principal engineer at Google, lead on GDocs
Software Engineering Is Becoming Factory Engineering

spoken_segments.text: First, a little bit about me. I've been an engineer for a long time. I was a principal engineer at Google. I used to lead engineering on the Google Docs suite, helped scale that product to hundreds of millions of users.
I'm currently the founder and CEO of Warp. Warp builds a platform for companies to build their own internal software factories. I'm going to show a little bit of that today.

Warp is also well known for our open source Agentic terminal, has about 65,000 GitHub stars. It's used by almost a million developers. Our mission has always been helping developers ship better software more quickly and it's cool to evolve what we're doing as the world changes around us.

scenes.alignment_note: Spoken background directly matches the bullet points listed under Zach Lloyd's name.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide showing a photograph of a multi-monitor developer desk setup representing local multi-threaded interactive prompting.
ocr_details: Software Engineering Is Becoming Factory Engineering

spoken_segments.text: This is where I think we're still mostly at. Most developers that I talk to, most platform teams, they're working with individuals who are running their own coding agents locally. Maybe they're running multiple of them at a time. It could be through their terminal, it could be through an agentic development environment.
Just show of hands quickly, actually, how many people in here are mostly working in this fashion, local multi threading? Okay, so still most people but actually not everyone.

scenes.alignment_note: The desk photo visually illustrates the 'local multi threading' and interactive prompting approach discussed.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide listing three key arguments for why the industry is shifting towards cloud software factories.
ocr_details: 2 Centralization for measuring and improving quality and cost
3 Security and governance in the cloud

spoken_segments.text: I think that this is going to change and it's starting to change already. The reasons are there's a few of them.

So one is like, if you are doing local interactive prompting as your main way of working with coding agents, you're kind of limited by human throughput really. Like you cannot automate if every agent needs to be interactively prompted.

There's a second reason too that I hear a lot from platform teams, and from engineering leaders. This mechanism of like everyone choosing their own local setup, their own models, their own skills. It makes it very hard to actually make sure that you're using these agents efficiently from like a cost perspective and a productivity perspective.
And then finally, there's like a big security problem and governance problem when everyone is setting up and running their own local agents.

scenes.alignment_note: Points 1, 2, and 3 on screen correspond directly to the speaker's discussion of human throughput limits, cost centralization, and cloud governance.

scenes.screen_title: What a software factory is not:
scenes.visual_summary: Slide featuring four boxes marked with red crosses indicating common misconceptions about software factories.
ocr_details: What a software factory is not:
A shared skills and mcp setup

spoken_segments.text: I'm going to define what I think of as a software factory, but I'll start by saying what I think a software factory is not.

I think it's not just a loose set of automations. I don't think of a software factory as a collection of AI teammates. I don't think it's a shared set of skills and MCPs, and I also don't think software factories are personal agent swarms. I think these are all useful primitives, but they're not the end state that we should be shooting for.

scenes.alignment_note: The four crossed-out cards on screen align item-by-item with the speaker's enumeration.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide displaying Zach's formal definition of a software factory highlighted in yellow background text.
ocr_details: A code-defined, closed-loop system for continuously measuring and improving cloud coding agents.

spoken_segments.text: And so, to me, the way that I define software factory is very specific. I define it as a code-defined closed loop system for continuously measuring and improving cloud coding agents.

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker reads the verbatim highlighted definition shown on the slide.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide explaining 'Factories as code' on the left alongside a YAML code configuration snippet defining a factory on the right.

spoken_segments.text: I believe the first thing you need to do is fully encode it in a declarative language. So you need to say, okay, these are all of the coding agents that I want to run, these are how they're triggered. When work comes into this factory, this is the workflow from triage to spec, whatever your workflow is.
You need to specify what MCPs are available, where your agents run. Really, as much as you can in a Terraform style declarative set of code files that define your factory.

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker points out specifying agents, triggers, and MCPs in a Terraform-like declarative code format while showing YAML snippet.

spoken_segments.text: The second part of it is a continuous closed loop of improvement. And that closed loop can look something like this. This is the typical one. This is just really the SDLC, where you have ideas that come in from people... and then your agents do some amount of work.
The important piece here is really this closed loop concept, where the more that your agents run, the more efficient you can make this loop.

spoken_segments.text: The third really key aspect, if you're building a software factory, is that everything needs to be measurable. If you're just going on vibes in terms of how you deploy coding agents, you can't be confident that you're actually getting the best, highest quality outputs, at the best cost.

scenes.alignment_note: The 'Measurement > Vibes' header and chart contrast empirical benchmark metrics against subjective feelings.

scenes.screen_title: Prompt your agents. Manage your agents. Engineer your agents.
scenes.visual_summary: Blue slide presenting three evolution stages of working with agents, emphasizing 'Engineer your agents.' in bold white.

spoken_segments.text: And so, if there's one thing that I'm hoping people walk away from this talk with, it's the idea that the way to work with coding agents and the way to think about them is that there's a really cool fundamental new engineering problem, which is How do you take this magic new primitive that we all have... and how do you engineer a system around them to use them most effectively?
When you think of coding agents as a new engineering primitive, then you naturally start to build a certain way of using them. That's the mindset.

scenes.alignment_note: The speaker emphasizes 'Engineer your agents' as the key thesis takeaway.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide detailing two foundational principles of the factory engineering mindset.
ocr_details: 1 Measure everything yourself based on your own data

spoken_segments.text: That's the mindset. So yeah, just to unpack that a bit, so there's continual measurement and continual learning.

scenes.alignment_note: Bullet points 1 and 2 summarize measurement and continuous improvement.

scenes.visual_summary: Slide listing core tool categories available to factory engineers.

spoken_segments.text: But there's also a new set of tools... In the new world of factory engineering, there's a new set of tools that everyone should be trying to master. And so those are things like, evals, it's can you set up self-improvement loops that work. Can you write benchmarks? Can you A/B test your factory?

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker explicitly lists the tools shown horizontally across the slide (Evals, self-improvement, benchmarks, A/B tests).

scenes.visual_summary: Slide contrasting Product engineering ('Building the product') with Factory engineering ('Improving the factory that builds the product').
ocr_details: Factory engineering = Improving the factory that builds the product

spoken_segments.text: Now, that doesn't mean that that's the only kind of engineering you're going to be doing. You're still going to be doing product engineering, meaning, you as an engineer should still feel responsible for does the product you ship actually solve a real user problem.
But the best engineers... is going to need to learn this new tool set of how do you improve the system, not just build the product.

scenes.alignment_note: Distinction between building the product vs. improving the system/factory aligns directly with the definitions on screen.

spoken_segments.text: And so what does that look like? If you think from first principles about how do you engineer an agentic system. I think you come up with something like this, doesn't have to be exactly this, but it's kind of an infrastructure stack that you're going to want to use...

At the bottom of this is what I call factories as code... Above that is a layer of data and context... On top of that is the compute layer... Above that is the inference layer... On top of that, you need an orchestration layer... And then finally, your factory should be all API and MCP first...

scenes.alignment_note: Speaker walks through each layer of the pyramid from bottom (00 Factories-as-code) to top (06 Access).

spoken_segments.text: The second thing, moving up a layer is the idea that everything that you do in the factory should be tracked across your entire team.
This is a sort of Google Docs style live view of what every coding agent on Warp's team across all of our engineers are doing at all times.
And so I could click in and I could see, Maggie is implementing Opus 55 on the high plan. She's doing it from Slack. It has this artifact, I could look in and see the actual conversation here.

spoken_segments.text: And then, there's this next layer of data, which is also really important that I mentioned earlier, which is the ability to set up online Evals that run across all your coding agent sessions.
So, it's like we have an eval score here that we use that is looking for redundant tests... one common failure mode of coding agents is that sometimes they will write tests that are unnecessary.

spoken_segments.text: Once you have that in place, You can do something that we call self-improvement which is rather than having humans look at the outputs of these scorers you have agents look at the output.

So this is like the awesome thing about having your factory defined as code and being able to use coding agents is that you can then have the coding agents diagnose problems with how they're working internally and suggest fixes to them.

spoken_segments.text: The final tool that I'm going to point out that I mentioned earlier is the ability to create and run benchmarks. This is also essential...
The only way to answer those questions for real is to test on your own data. And so you should have in place some mechanism where you can basically create a benchmark set out of your real data...
This is something that looks like what you might get when a new model drops, like in Sweetbench or Terminal Bench. It's showing the trade-offs of different models here in terms of cost and quality...
